item.research_question: Can high-entropy effects be utilized to induce a significant glass-to-glass transition in metallic glasses, and what are the structural and thermodynamic mechanisms behind this phenomenon?
item.material_system: Equiatomic NbNiZrTiCo high-entropy metallic glass (HEMG), with comparative systems NbNiZrTiCu and NbNiZrTiCoCu
item.processing_route: Arc melting of pure elements (Nb, Ni, Zr, Ti, Co, Cu; purity ≥ 99.9 wt.%) under high-purity argon, followed by remelting five times; ribbon production via melt-spinning at a wheel surface velocity of 32 m s−1; heat treatment by heating to 855 K (TA) at 20 K min−1 and cooling at 20 K min−1
item.test_conditions: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) at heating rates of 10–50 K min−1 and Flash DSC at >1000 K s−1; in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction from 305 K to 803 K at 30 K min−1; nanoindentation; dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA); atom probe tomography (APT) at 65 K; high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) at 200 kV
key_findings: The as-prepared NbNiZrTiCo HEMG exhibits an enormous exothermic peak at 781 K with a heat release of 1.65 kJ mol−1, which is approximately 130% of the subsequent crystallization exotherm (1.27 kJ mol−1).

The glass-to-glass transition is irreversible; the heat-treated sample shows a distinct glass transition temperature (Tg) at ~764 K and lacks the first exothermic peak observed in the as-prepared state.
Nanoindentation measurements reveal a drastic increase in hardness from 6.78 GPa to 9.46 GPa (approximately 40% increase) after the transition.

In-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction shows a significant non-linear shift of the first peak in the total structure function S(Q) and a narrowing of the full width at half maximum (FWHM) during the transition.

Pair-distribution function (G(r)) analysis indicates a contraction of short-range atomic distances (r11 and r12 shift to low-r) and prominent splitting of the second peak, signifying enhanced short- and medium-range ordering.
Atom probe tomography confirms a uniform element distribution at the sub-nanometer scale in both as-prepared and heat-treated samples, excluding spinodal decomposition.
The calculated lower limit of entropy change (ΔSH−L) for the transition is −1.96 J mol−1 K−1, with a corresponding enthalpy change (ΔHH−L) of −1.65 kJ mol−1.
Substituting Co with Cu to form NbNiZrTiCu (maintaining high excess configurational entropy) and adding Cu to form NbNiZrTiCoCu both result in similar glass-to-glass transitions.
item.mechanism: The authors propose that the high configurational entropy (SC) and high excess configurational entropy (SE) dynamically stabilize a high-energy glass state during rapid vitrification by hindering atomic reconstruction and slowing diffusion. Upon heating, this high-energy state undergoes a thermodynamically driven transition to a low-energy, more ordered glass state, releasing a large amount of heat. The transition is driven by the specific combination of high SC and high SE (related to atomic size misfit), which enables the formation of a high-energy glass that is distinct from conventional metallic glasses.
item.limitations: The text notes that the observed phase transition is an irreversible process, meaning the calculated entropy change represents a lower limit. Additionally, the detailed structural changes cannot be fully resolved by atom probe tomography due to its limited spatial resolution, and some weak diffraction peaks in crystallized samples could not be identified.
item.future_work: The authors suggest that the HEMGs may serve as model materials for exploring glass-to-glass transitions and the fundamental nature of glasses in materials science and condensed-matter physics. They also propose potential applications as energetic materials due to the large anomalous exotherm, which could contribute to combustion heats and lower ignition temperatures.
quotes: An unusual glass-to-glass phase transition is discovered during heating with an enormous heat release even larger than that of the following crystallization at higher temperatures.
The exotherm of NbNiZrTiCo HEMG is ~130% of the following crystallization exotherm, resulting in a unique glass-to-glass transition.

The high-entropy effect could dynamically elevate the MG to a high-energy glass state and thermodynamically enable the glass-to-glass transition from the high-energy glass state to a low-energy glass state during heating.
